scholarly_quality.concise_summary: While the empirical exploration of coding agents in physical robotics is detailed and offers valuable qualitative insights, the experimental rigor is undermined by reporting development-stage cumulative success rather than isolated held-out evaluations of final policies, along with unmatched seed baselines in simulation benchmarks. Given these methodological and evaluation uncertainties, an uncertain verdict is appropriate.

Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable
robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot
capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement
(RSI) throughreal-worldexploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a
framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable
executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places
physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate,

an embodied RSI framework for this study (Figure 1). A researcher agent selects experimental objectives and
technicalapproaches, whileanengineeragentimplementsprograms, executesrobottrials, anddiagnosesfailures.
Their interaction connects local code improvement with task-level reassessment. A persistent repository records
environmental facts, attempted approaches, execution outcomes, and reusable implementations, allowing
later experiments to build on earlier experience while model parameters remain fixed. For deployment, the
resulting code can be frozen and executed without runtime language-model calls, while still responding to live
observations through its perception, control, and recovery routines. This separation enables us to study both
the process of developing robot capabilities and the behavior of the programs that retain them.

Our experiments cover eight manipulation tasks on a dual-arm Franka platform, spanning reasoning, long-
horizon execution, precise contact, deformable objects, and bimanual coordination. Recorded development
success averages 91.1% across tasks. These rates aggregate attempts across code revisions; frozen-program
performance is evaluated separately. Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo tasks yields 84.82% success,
averaged equally over five capability groups, compared with reported results of 50.35% for PyRUA-Lean and
22.48% for GPT-6-Astra. Our main contributions can be summarized as:

parameters held fixed, the system develops task programs through code generation, testing, and feedback

evidence.excerpt:
Physical exploration produces agent-free programs for seven of the eight tasks (Figure 5). These programs
execute using live perception, control, and recovery logic without runtime language-model calls. Approximate
time to first success ranges from 1.5 hours for block storage to 45 hours for Push T, indicating substantial
variation in acquisition cost across tasks. Ethernet insertion remains unsuccessful without online agent
participation in the reported development record.
Across the seven tasks with agent-free solutions, recorded development success ranges from 91.67% to 100%
(Figure 5b). These rates aggregate attempts across program revisions and describe the development record
rather than the reliability of a single frozen program. Successful execution times also vary substantially across
tasks (Figure 5c); their task-specific endpoints are defined in Appendix C.

Method selection can limit self-improvement.The deadlocks in Section 4.4 suggest that progress
can be limited by which methods an agent considers. Depth and calibration errors constrained geometric
localization: stacking progressed with local visual alignment and contact feedback, while Hanoi combined
coarse localization with wrist-camera feedback. In simulated general pickup, success improved after a human
suggested SigLIP, a visual model the agent had initially overlooked. These cases indicate that the ability
to implement and refine a method does not ensure that useful alternatives will be explored. A practical
implication is to include explicit comparisons of alternative perception and control strategies when the current
approach repeatedly fails.

methods considered during exploration. Human input also resolved

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Frozen programs are later evaluated on held-out RoboDojo layouts and deployment-time efficiency is compared against online baselines, providing partially independent corroboration, but headline physical success rates derive from development-stage rollouts.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Headline claims of high autonomous success (e.g., 91.1% on real-world tasks) conflict with the fact that these metrics include cumulative development attempts rather than rigorous held-out test evaluations. Furthermore, highly contact-rich tasks like Ethernet insertion failed without online agent and human intervention, which the authors acknowledge in the discussion.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation combines 8 real-world physical manipulation tasks on a dual-arm Franka robot with 42 simulated tasks on the RoboDojo benchmark. However, the reported physical success rates aggregate development attempts across changing code versions rather than testing frozen policies under controlled, randomized trials, and several RoboDojo comparisons rely on unmatched seeds from leaderboard snapshots.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The authors evaluate final frozen programs on held-out layout sets in simulation (RoboDojo) and compare execution times against online baselines.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: For real-world tasks, headline metrics reflect aggregated success across development-stage rollouts; for simulation, evaluation is scored on RoboDojo benchmark tasks.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: The engineer and researcher agents iteratively refine code using execution logs, camera frames, and physical trial outcomes.

primary.limitations: The authors transparently report limitations, including that offline programs can fail on unseen variations, contact-rich tasks often require online intervention, and human guidance was used during exploration deadlocks.
primary.method_assessment: The framework separates roles between a researcher agent specifying objectives and an engineer agent performing code generation, diagnosis, and local refinements across physical and simulated environments. While architectural and workflow details are explained clearly, the development process involves human interventions (e.g., suggesting vision models or resolving deadlocks), and the physical iteration traces often reflect ad-hoc repairs rather than fully autonomous, repeatable optimization pipelines.
primary.quality_rationale: While the empirical exploration of coding agents in physical robotics is detailed and offers valuable qualitative insights, the experimental rigor is undermined by reporting development-stage cumulative success rather than isolated held-out evaluations of final policies, along with unmatched seed baselines in simulation benchmarks. Given these methodological and evaluation uncertainties, an uncertain verdict is appropriate.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper investigates embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) in real-world robotic manipulation and simulation using PyRUA-REAL, where collaborative coding agents iteratively develop, test, and refine robot programs that are retained in persistent memory and deployed offline without runtime LLM calls.
